doc.title: Joe Muranyi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007

title: Decline of live jazz in New York bars and clubs
summary: He explains how rents, TV and changing habits killed neighborhood jazz bars and clubs.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Yeah, yeah. But you know what happened, Monk, was that around New York, a big city like this, you know rent was fairly cheap, not like today, you know. The trouble with New York today is there are too many people with too much money. And in those days rent was reasonable, a lot of little restaurants, clubs, bars, bars would have little bands. Weekends if nothing else. Or Ryan’s started as a bar, that went on for years, that wasn’t supposed to be a jazz nightclub or anything. So that just sort of all disappeared. And nothing has replaced it. And T.V. killed a lot of this stuff. You know why go into a local bar and have a few beers and listen to the band when you can see the famous names and Milton Berle on television. So I think everything has mitigated against live jazz. I mean live jazz was associated ad infinitum, ad nauseum, way back with a club and drinking and dancing. You know, I mean times have changed and they’re changing around. But right now in New York there aren’t that many jazz clubs.
And it costs a lot to go to them often times.
